summary:
ASTRA (Astronaut Health Insight) is a prototype astronaut health-monitoring and intelligence platform designed to support safer, more informed human spaceflight. Long-duration missions expose astronauts to health challenges associated with altered gravity, radiation, isolation, sleep disruption and other demanding environmental conditions.

ASTRA brings together wearable-based biometric observations, daily health check-ins, personal health trends, structured assessments, mission environmental context and NASA research resources in one connected workspace. Its prototype wearable architecture uses an ESP32 microcontroller with MAX30102 optical sensing and temperature sensing to demonstrate biometric data acquisition. The platform compares available observations with personal baselines, identifies questionable or insufficient data, and supports traceable follow-up and authorised medical review.

By connecting individual observations with scientific evidence and mission context, ASTRA aims to make astronaut health information easier to understand, monitor and review throughout a mission. It is a research prototype, not a flight-qualified medical device or autonomous diagnostic system.
details:
Project Overview

ASTRA (Astronaut Health Insight) is a connected astronaut health-monitoring and intelligence prototype developed to explore how health observations, scientific research and mission environmental context can be brought together to support human spaceflight.

Long-duration space missions introduce complex challenges to human health and performance. Altered gravity, radiation exposure, isolation, sleep disruption and demanding spacecraft environments can affect multiple physiological systems. ASTRA addresses this challenge by providing a structured environment for collecting, monitoring, analysing and reviewing astronaut health information.

How ASTRA Works

ASTRA is built around an integrated health-monitoring workflow:

1. Wearable Biometric Monitoring

The prototype wearable architecture combines an ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30102 optical sensor and temperature sensing to demonstrate the acquisition and transmission of biometric observations. The platform distinguishes prototype hardware capabilities from planned or unavailable measurements.

2. Daily Health Check-ins

Astronauts can record health observations, symptoms, fatigue, sleep and wellbeing information. These records provide additional context alongside available sensor measurements.

3. Personal Health Trends

ASTRA organises historical observations and compares available measurements against personal baselines. It provides trend visualisation, measurement history and data-quality context to help identify changes over time.

4. Structured Health Assessments

Configured assessment rules evaluate available observations and identify potential changes, questionable readings or insufficient data. Each assessment retains its supporting information and follow-up status. Assessment outcomes are review prompts, not medical diagnoses.

5. AI Medical Assistant

The AI-assisted interface retrieves authorised health records and available scientific resources to help users understand recorded observations and relevant research. It operates within defined safety limitations and does not independently diagnose, prescribe or replace medical professionals.

6. NASA Research and Evidence

ASTRA connects relevant NASA research resources, including the Human Research Program, Human Research Roadmap, NASA Technical Reports Server, Open Science Data Repository and radiation research resources. This allows users to explore scientific context while keeping external research datasets separate from individual astronaut measurements.

7. Medical Review and Handoff

The platform supports traceable assessment records, review statuses and follow-up workflows for authorised medical personnel. Automated findings remain distinct from human medical decisions.

8. Mission Environmental Context

The Mission Environment workspace presents environmental observations such as temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, oxygen, pressure and radiation context. Environmental records remain separate from personal health measurements.

Technology and Development Tools

The prototype combines web technologies, database-backed services, hardware components and external research resources.

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Backend: PHP.
  • Database: MySQL.
  • Local development environment: XAMPP.
  • Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30102 optical sensor and temperature sensor.
  • External research: NASA HRP, HRR, NTRS, OSDR, RadLab and DONKI resources.
  • Additional research integration: Canadian Space Agency open-data resources.
  • Development assistance: AI-assisted programming and development tools.

Innovation and Creativity

ASTRA's central innovation is its attempt to connect several important parts of astronaut health support into one coherent workflow rather than presenting isolated measurements.

It brings together wearable observations, personal baselines, structured assessments, scientific evidence, mission environmental context and human medical review.

It also emphasises data provenance and quality: simulated observations are labelled, questionable readings are retained, insufficient data is not interpreted as normal, and external research is not presented as personal medical evidence.

Intended Impact

ASTRA aims to demonstrate how connected health information and evidence-based context could support astronaut self-monitoring, improve visibility into changes over time and facilitate more structured medical review during long-duration missions.

The prototype is intended as a foundation for further development, hardware validation, scientific evaluation and future integration with more advanced space-health monitoring technologies.

ASTRA is not a flight-qualified medical device, does not provide autonomous medical diagnoses and has not been clinically validated. Its demonstration includes simulated data where actual hardware measurements are unavailable.
